827.title: Mus'ab ibn Umayr
827.hook: a rich, perfumed youth who gave everything up and died at Uhud with a shroud too short
827.howItsDone: Muslims retell the story of Mus'ab ibn Umayr, from the hadith of Khabbab and of Abdur-Rahman ibn Awf in Sahih al-Bukhari, as a reminder of what the early believers gave up.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ammar ibn Yasir, forced under torture to say words against his faith, and told that what counted was his heart. Your line was: the heart held. Did you go easier on yourself for one weak moment? Day eight hundred twenty-seven.

A man who is fasting is brought his food at the end of the day, and he cannot eat it. Abdur-Rahman ibn Awf, a companion who had become wealthy, sits looking at the meal and starts to remember a friend. Mus'ab ibn Umayr was killed, he says, and he was better than me. All we had to wrap him in was one cloak. If we covered his head, his feet showed. If we covered his feet, his head showed. Then he says the hard thing: now the world has been spread out for us, and I am afraid our good deeds were paid back early. And he weeps, and leaves the food where it is. Today: the young man in the short cloak.
screen: `A MEAL HE CANNOT EAT.` → `ONE CLOAK FOR A FRIEND.` → `WERE WE PAID BACK EARLY?`

segments.voice: The biographers remember Mus'ab as a young man from a comfortable Meccan family, well dressed and well perfumed, the kind people noticed in the street. Tradition says his mother cut him off when he became Muslim. A report in Tirmidhi tells of a day he walked in wearing a cloak patched with leather, and the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, wept, remembering how he used to live. Later, tradition says, the Prophet sent him ahead to Medina. Sahih al-Bukhari records the people of Medina saying that Mus'ab came to them with another companion, teaching them the Qur'an, before the Prophet himself arrived. So the young man who had everything became a teacher in a city that was not his own. Then Uhud. Mus'ab was killed in that battle. And here a second companion, Khabbab, tells what happened next, also in Bukhari. Some of us, Khabbab says, died before taking any of their reward in this world, and Mus'ab was one of them. He left nothing but a striped woolen cloak. When they covered his head, his feet were bare. When they covered his feet, his head was bare. So the Prophet told them: cover his head, and lay some sweet-smelling grass, idhkhir, over his feet. Hold those two pictures side by side. A youth known for his perfume, and a body covered at the feet with wild grass. Khabbab sets him against those who lived on and saw their fruit ripen. Mus'ab never saw it ripen. And Abdur-Rahman, years later, at a full table, could not eat for thinking about him. The short cloak became a measure. Not a judgment on wealth, since Abdur-Rahman was wealthy too and is honored, but a question he kept asking himself: what was given up, and what was kept back?
screen: `THE WELL-PERFUMED YOUNG MAN.` · `A TEACHER SENT TO MEDINA.` · `KILLED AT UHUD WITH ONE CLOAK.` · `GRASS LAID OVER HIS FEET.` · then, large: `THE SHROUD WAS TOO SHORT.`

segments.voice: The practice: give up one luxury. Settle, and breathe. Run through the small comforts in your day. The extra coffee, the scrolling before sleep, the second dessert, the thing in your cart you don't need. Choose one, just for today. Not as a punishment. As a way of noticing how much you are carrying. Breathe in, and picture it set down. Breathe out, and picture the space it leaves. If you pray, you can give thanks for what you have and ask for a heart that holds it lightly. The bell holds the time.
Mus'ab ibn Umayr. The young man who left comfort behind, taught the Qur'an in Medina, and was buried at Uhud in a cloak that could not cover him. Today's word.
Your line: the shroud was too short. Today, set down one luxury, and notice what you reach for in its place. Day eight hundred twenty-seven.

828.title: Zayd ibn Harithah
828.hook: the only companion named in the Qur'an (33:37)
828.howItsDone: Muslims learn Zayd ibn Harithah's story from the sira and from Surah al-Ahzab, where verse 37 names him; reciters say his name whenever they reach that verse.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mus'ab ibn Umayr, buried at Uhud with grass over his feet. Your line was: the shroud was too short. Which luxury did you set down, and what did you reach for instead? Day eight hundred twenty-eight.

Read the Qur'an from cover to cover and you meet prophets by name: Abraham, Moses, Jesus, Joseph. You meet Pharaoh. You meet Mary. The men and women around the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, are another matter. The book speaks about them, to them, and of what they did, often without saying who. And then, in the thirty-third surah, one plain name appears. Not a king. Not a prophet. A man who came into the Prophet's house as a slave. Tradition says he is the only companion the Qur'an names. Today: Zayd.
screen: `PROPHETS BY NAME.` → `COMPANIONS, MOSTLY UNNAMED.` → `ONE NAME IN SURAH 33.`

segments.voice: Start with how Zayd came. The biographies tell that he was taken as a boy and sold, and ended up in Khadijah's household, and she gave him to Muhammad before the revelation began. Muhammad freed him. The same biographies tell a story: Zayd's father and uncle tracked him down and came to buy him back, and Zayd was given the choice to go home. He chose to stay. That story comes from the sira, not from the Qur'an or Bukhari, so hold it as a story the tradition tells. What Bukhari does record is what people called him. Abdullah ibn Umar said: we used to call him Zayd ibn Muhammad, Zayd son of Muhammad, until the verse came telling believers to call adopted children by their real fathers. That is in the same surah, verse five. And a little later, verse forty says, in Pickthall's words: "Muhammad is not the father of any man among you." So Zayd lost a name. He went back to being Zayd ibn Harithah, son of his own father. And in that same surah, he gained another. Verse thirty-seven speaks to the Prophet about Zayd's marriage to Zaynab and its ending, and in the middle of it the text says his name: Zayd. It is a hard passage, about a marriage that did not hold and a custom being changed, and commentators read it carefully. But notice what happened to the freed boy. People had called him the son of the Prophet. The book took that title away, and then it wrote his own name into revelation. The book that names prophets also names him. Whenever someone recites that verse, his name is said aloud.
screen: `A BOY SOLD, THEN FREED.` · `CALLED ZAYD SON OF MUHAMMAD.` · `CALL THEM BY THEIR FATHERS.` · `HIS NAME IN VERSE 37.` · then, large: `NAMED IN THE BOOK.`

segments.voice: The practice: learn his story. Settle, and breathe. Go back over what you just heard, slowly, as if you will tell it to someone tonight. A boy taken from home. A household that freed him. A name people gave him. A verse that gave him back his father's name. A verse that says his own. Breathe in on each step, breathe out between them. Then, if you have a Qur'an nearby, or an app, you might find surah thirty-three, verse thirty-seven, and look for his name on the page. If you pray, you can ask for those who were taken from home. The bell holds the time.
Zayd ibn Harithah. Freed by the Prophet, once called his son, given back his father's name, and named in the Qur'an at surah thirty-three, verse thirty-seven. Today's word.
Your line: named in the book. Today, call someone by their real name, carefully and correctly, especially someone people usually overlook. Day eight hundred twenty-eight.

829.title: Usamah ibn Zayd
829.hook: appointed a general at around eighteen, over senior men
829.howItsDone: Muslims tell the story of Usamah ibn Zayd's command from Sahih al-Bukhari, where the Prophet answers those who doubted the young leader by pointing to his father.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Zayd ibn Harithah, the freed man whose name is written in surah thirty-three. Your line was: named in the book. Whose name did you take care to say right? Day eight hundred twenty-nine.

The name of the new commander goes around the camp in Medina. Older men hear it and frown. They have fought for years. They were there at the hard beginnings. And the one put in charge of them is young enough to be their son. People start to talk. Is this really the right choice? The talk reaches the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. He stands up to answer it. Today: the son of yesterday's Zayd.
screen: `A COMMANDER IS NAMED.` → `OLDER MEN FROWN.` → `THE TALK REACHES THE PROPHET.`

segments.voice: Usamah was the son of Zayd ibn Harithah, the man we met yesterday, and tradition remembers him as very young when he was given command. Sahih al-Bukhari keeps what happened when the grumbling started. Abdullah ibn Umar reports that the Prophet sent out an army and made Usamah its leader, and some people found fault with his leadership. So the Prophet answered them. If you find fault with his leadership, he said, you found fault with his father's leadership before him. By God, his father was fit to lead, and he was among the people dearest to me, and this son is among the people dearest to me after him. Notice what the answer does. It does not say: he's young, but give him a chance. It ties Usamah to his father, a freed man who had also been doubted, and says both were fit. The objection is treated as an old habit showing up again, not as wisdom. And it puts love on the record, out loud, in front of the men who were complaining. Tradition adds that the army had not yet left when the Prophet died, and that Abu Bakr, soon after, sent it out under Usamah anyway, as it had been planned. There is a nickname the tradition gives him: the beloved, son of the beloved. Young, and trusted. The trust did not wait for him to get older. It was given first, and then it was defended.
screen: `THE SON OF ZAYD.` · `SOME FOUND FAULT WITH HIS LEADERSHIP.` · `YOU DOUBTED HIS FATHER TOO.` · `FIT TO LEAD, AND DEAR TO ME.` · then, large: `YOUNG AND TRUSTED.`

segments.voice: The practice: trust a young person. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone younger than you. A child, a niece, a student, a new colleague, the junior person in the group chat. Think of one thing they could do that you usually do yourself, or check twice. Breathe in, and picture handing it over. Breathe out, and picture not checking. Notice anything that resists. Then think how you would speak up for them if someone else doubted them. If you pray, you can ask for wisdom for the young people around you. The bell holds the time.
Usamah ibn Zayd. The young son of a freed man, given command over older companions, and defended by the Prophet as fit to lead. Today's word.
Your line: young and trusted. Today, hand one real responsibility to someone younger, and if anyone doubts them, say why you trust them. Day eight hundred twenty-nine.

830.title: Umm Ayman
830.hook: the woman who nursed the baby Muhammad ﷺ, whom he called my mother after my mother
830.howItsDone: Muslims remember Umm Ayman as the Prophet's nurse and the mother of Usamah, and retell the report in Sahih Muslim of Abu Bakr and Umar visiting her after his death.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Usamah ibn Zayd, the young commander the Prophet defended in public. Your line was: young and trusted. What did you hand over, and did you let it go? Day eight hundred thirty.

Two leaders of Medina walk to the house of an old woman. One is Abu Bakr, the new leader of the community. The other is Umar. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, has died, and Abu Bakr says to Umar: come, let us visit Umm Ayman, the way the Prophet used to visit her. They knock. They sit with her. And she begins to cry. Before we hear why, it helps to know who she was, and why the Prophet kept going to her door. Today: Umm Ayman.
screen: `TWO LEADERS AT HER DOOR.` → `AS THE PROPHET USED TO VISIT.` → `SHE BEGINS TO CRY.`

segments.voice: Her name, tradition says, was Barakah. A note in Sahih Muslim, from the early scholar Ibn Shihab, describes her plainly. She came from Abyssinia, she served in the household of Muhammad's father, and after his father died she looked after the baby until he was grown. She was the mother of Usamah. Nursed here means cared for and carried, not breastfed; his milk-mothers were other women. So yesterday's young commander was her son, and Zayd ibn Harithah was her husband. Tradition says that when Muhammad's mother died on a journey, it was Umm Ayman who brought the little boy home, and that years later he would say of her: she is my mother after my mother. That line comes from the biographies, so hold it as the tradition's memory. What Muslim records firmly is the visit. Abu Bakr and Umar come to her house after the Prophet's death. She weeps, and they try to comfort her. Don't you know, they say, that what is with God is better for His Messenger? And she answers: I know that. That is not why I am crying. I am crying because the revelation from heaven has stopped. And her answer, the report says, moved them to tears as well, and they wept with her. Look at the shape of it. The woman who carried the baby is the one who understands, before anyone says it, what has ended. The leaders came to comfort her, and she ended up teaching them. And they came because he used to come. Honoring the woman who raised him did not end with his death. It went on, through a visit.
screen: `BARAKAH, FROM ABYSSINIA.` · `SHE CARED FOR THE BABY MUHAMMAD.` · `ABU BAKR AND UMAR VISIT HER.` · `THE REVELATION HAS STOPPED.` · then, large: `MY MOTHER AFTER MY MOTHER.`

segments.voice: The practice: thank a caregiver. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who looked after you when you were small, or when you were sick, or when you were new somewhere. A grandmother, a nanny, an aunt, a neighbor, a nurse, a teacher. Maybe not a parent. Maybe someone the world didn't call family. Breathe in, and remember one specific thing they did. Breathe out, and say thank you in your mind. If they're living, think about how you might tell them. If they've died, and you pray, you can ask mercy for them. The bell holds the time.
Umm Ayman. The woman who nursed and cared for the baby Muhammad, mother of Usamah, visited by the Prophet and, after him, by Abu Bakr and Umar. Today's word.

831.title: Ja'far the flyer
831.hook: killed at Mu'tah holding the banner, told he had two wings in the garden (Bukhari)
831.howItsDone: Muslims call Ja'far ibn Abi Talib al-Tayyar, the flyer, and Dhul-Janahayn, the one with two wings, and retell the account of Mu'tah from Sahih al-Bukhari.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Umm Ayman, the Prophet's nurse, who wept because revelation had stopped. Your line was: my mother after my mother. Did you thank someone who cared for you? Day eight hundred thirty-one.

In Medina, Abdullah ibn Umar meets a man in the street and greets him with a strange name. Peace be upon you, he says, son of the one with two wings. He is the son of Ja'far, the Prophet's cousin, and his father is dead. Every time Ibn Umar met him, Bukhari says, he greeted him that way. Not son of the martyr. Not son of the brave. Son of the one with two wings. To understand the greeting, you have to go to a battlefield, to a banner, and to the moment it passed from one hand to the next. Today: Ja'far.
screen: `A GREETING IN THE STREET.` → `SON OF THE ONE WITH TWO WINGS.` → `BACK TO A BATTLEFIELD.`

segments.voice: Ja'far ibn Abi Talib was Ali's brother and a cousin of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. Years before, tradition says, he had led the believers who took refuge in Abyssinia and spoke for them before its Christian king. Now an army is sent north, to a place called Mu'tah. Bukhari records how the Prophet set the command: Zayd ibn Harithah leads. If Zayd is killed, Ja'far. If Ja'far is killed, Abdullah ibn Rawahah. Three names, in order, each ready to take what the one before let fall. Then, in Medina, before any messenger had come back, the Prophet stood and gave the news, with tears in his eyes, Bukhari says. Zayd took the banner and was killed. Then Ja'far took it and was killed. Then Ibn Rawahah took it and was killed. And then, he said, one of the swords of God took it, and God gave them victory. Tradition adds the detail people remember: that Ja'far held the banner in his right hand until it was cut, then in his left, then held it to his chest with what was left of his arms. That part comes from the biographies. What the hadith collections keep is the answer. A report in Tirmidhi has the Prophet saying he saw Ja'far flying in the garden with the angels. And so Ibn Umar greets the son as son of the two-winged one. The arms he lost holding the banner, tradition says, were given back as wings. The banner passed from hand to hand, and each held it to the end. Two wings.
screen: `THE PROPHET'S COUSIN.` · `ZAYD, THEN JA'FAR, THEN IBN RAWAHAH.` · `THE BANNER PASSES HAND TO HAND.` · `FLYING IN THE GARDEN.` · then, large: `TWO WINGS.`

segments.voice: The practice: hold on to one duty. Settle, and breathe. Think of the things you carry for other people. A child's ride to school. A parent's medicine. A promise at work. A prayer you keep. Choose one that has started to slip. Breathe in, and picture taking it up again, in your right hand. Breathe out, and picture keeping hold of it through one ordinary, tiring day. Not every duty. Just this one. If you pray, you can ask for steadiness to carry it. The bell holds the time.
Ja'far the flyer. Ja'far ibn Abi Talib, who took the banner at Mu'tah after Zayd fell and was killed holding it, and whom the tradition calls the one with two wings. Today's word.
Your line: two wings. Today, pick up the one duty you chose and carry it through to the end of the day. Day eight hundred thirty-one.

832.title: Abdullah ibn Mas'ud
832.hook: the shepherd boy who became one of the great reciters (Bukhari)
832.howItsDone: Muslims learn about Abdullah ibn Mas'ud as a teacher of the Qur'an, and retell the hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari where the Prophet asked him to recite and wept at Surat an-Nisa.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ja'far, who took up the banner at Mu'tah and was called the one with two wings. Your line was: two wings. Which duty did you hold on to all day? Day eight hundred thirty-two.

Recite to me. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says it to one of his companions, and the man is startled. Recite to you? he asks. When it was revealed to you? The Prophet answers: I love to hear it from someone else. So the man opens his mouth and begins. The one being asked is not a chief or a merchant. He is a man who once, tradition says, looked after other people's sheep outside Mecca. Today: Abdullah ibn Mas'ud.
screen: `RECITE TO ME.` → `WHEN IT CAME TO YOU?` → `I LOVE TO HEAR IT FROM ANOTHER.`

segments.voice: Start with the hillside. A story in Musnad Ahmad tells that young Abdullah was tending a flock for one of the Meccan chiefs when the Prophet and Abu Bakr passed by and asked for milk. He said the sheep were not his to give. Hold on to that honesty; it is where the story begins. He became Muslim, and he stayed close to the Prophet, and he learned the Qur'an straight from his mouth. Sahih al-Bukhari records the Prophet naming the people to learn the Qur'an from, and Abdullah ibn Mas'ud is named in that short list. Ibn Mas'ud himself says, also in Bukhari, that there was no surah he did not know where it was revealed, and that if he knew anyone who knew the book better and could be reached by camel, he would ride to him. Sure of what he knew, and still hungry to learn more, in the same breath. Now back to the hook. When the Prophet asks him to recite, Bukhari says, he begins Surat an-Nisa. He reaches the verse that asks how it will be when a witness is brought from every people, and the Prophet brought as a witness over them. And the Prophet says: enough. Ibn Mas'ud looks up, and the Prophet's eyes are streaming with tears. The shepherd boy's voice carried the words, and the one who first received them wept to hear them from someone else. Not a voice on show. The text, carried until it landed.

833.title: Ubayy ibn Ka'b
833.hook: the master reciter, whom the Prophet ﷺ was told to recite to (Bukhari)
833.howItsDone: Muslims remember Ubayy ibn Ka'b as a reciter and scribe of the Qur'an, and retell the hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari in which the Prophet recited Surat al-Bayyinah to him at God's command.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, who recited Surat an-Nisa until the Prophet said enough. Your line was: the shepherd reciter. What did you say slowly, and well? Day eight hundred thirty-three.

Yesterday the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, asked a companion to recite to him. Today it runs the other way, and it is stranger. The Prophet comes to a man in Medina and says: God has commanded me to recite to you. Not to the whole community. To you. The man is Ubayy ibn Ka'b, and his first question is not about the surah. It is one breathless question about himself. Today: Ubayy.
screen: `YESTERDAY: RECITE TO ME.` → `TODAY: I WAS TOLD TO RECITE TO YOU.` → `ONE BREATHLESS QUESTION.`

segments.voice: Ubayy ibn Ka'b was one of the Ansar, the people of Medina, and he wrote down revelation for the Prophet. In the short list of people to learn the Qur'an from, the one we met yesterday, his name is there too. Sahih al-Bukhari keeps the scene. The Prophet says to him: God has commanded me to recite to you the surah that begins Lam yakun, the one known as al-Bayyinah, the Clear Proof. And Ubayy asks: did He name me? Yes, the Prophet says. And Ubayy weeps. Think about what he is asking. He knows the Qur'an deeply. He could recite this surah himself. In the report, what brings the tears is not the surah. It is being named, and having the words carried to him personally. A second scene, in Sahih Muslim, shows the other side of him. The Prophet tests him: which verse in the book of God that you have with you is the greatest? Ubayy answers: the verse of the Throne, Ayat al-Kursi. And the Prophet strikes him on the chest and says, may knowledge delight you. So here is a man who knew the text well enough to be quizzed, and who still wept to be recited to. Both are part of being a reciter. And this closes a week of early believers: Mus'ab's short shroud, Zayd's name in the book, Usamah young and trusted, Umm Ayman the mother after a mother, Ja'far's two wings, Ibn Mas'ud the shepherd reciter, and now Ubayy. Recite to him.

segments.voice: The practice: recite to a friend. Settle, and breathe. Think of one person you could share a short passage with today. A friend, a sibling, a child at bedtime. Choose what you'd say: a short surah, a line of a poem, a verse that matters to you. Breathe in, and say it once in your mind, slowly. Breathe out, and picture their face as they hear it. You are not performing. You are carrying something to them by name. If you pray, you can ask that the words reach them well. The bell holds the time.
